name: Zoe Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel, with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential; what happens on a usual shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I feed flat cardboard into a die-cutter that stamps box shapes and handle holes. I finished secondary school and am still junior on this machine, so I call the setter when a cut turns ragged. The pay is low, and the dusty feeder makes my shoulders ache by the end of a week.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is home like, and do you use AI?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Luc repairs roads, and we have two school-age children and a mortgage. We have less than a month of expenses saved and only a few similar factories nearby. I have never used AI; I keep the feeder steps on a paper card because new screens take me time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the canteen that our box cutter still needs someone to watch the feed. I have no AI app to talk about, and a tidy office report would not clear a jam.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The machine may carry on, but my wage barely covers the mortgage payment and food. My partner Luc works on road repairs, yet our two children cost more each year and we have less than one month saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep feeding the die-cutter and checking the first flat box after each setting. If a full week leaves anything after bills, I would put a new small amount from that pay into an emergency account, not promise a fixed amount I cannot meet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious even in the quiet version. A missed shift would put the mortgage payment on the kitchen table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a bad cut look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The handle hole leaves a ragged edge or the fold line misses the mark. I stop the feeder and call the setter, because I am still learning the adjustment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How often is money left after bills?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not every week. Luc and I would record the real amount after the mortgage, food and bus fare before transferring anything new.

say: I would tell the **box crew** that a jam still needs a person at the feeder.
I would keep **AI apps** out of work I do not understand.
think: My **low wage** and mortgage leave very little spare.
Less than **one month saved** makes a lost shift serious even if AI plateaus.
do: Feed the **die-cutter** and check the first flat box after each setting.
Save **new wages** only after essential bills leave a real surplus.
feel: **Anxious** about an ordinary missed shift and the mortgage.
S0.quote: A missed shift would put the mortgage payment on the kitchen table.
fieldNote: The plateau leaves Zoe’s **baseline money pressure** in place, with two school-age children and thin savings.
Her new saving is **conditional on surplus pay**, not a relabelled reserve or promised fixed transfer.

steps.text: Keep feeding the die-cutter and checking first boxes
Save fresh wages only when mortgage and essential bills leave a surplus

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the office can order cardboard faster if it wants, but somebody should still check each new shape. I would ask the supervisor before any camera decides a cut is good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A quicker schedule might take paid setup minutes off my shift, and a stacking robot could remove the simple work I do. I am junior, slow with new screens and one of the easier people to replace; my partner Luc’s road wage alone would not meet the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my shift and write down the paid setup time for four runs. If the new rota cuts my hours, we would cancel our summer trip and I would look at posted local packing jobs that pay enough for the mortgage; I would not leave for a rumour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, watching the noticeboard more than I should. I can make the spending cut, but there are few other factories close enough for the school run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a camera miss on a box blank?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A fold might be sharp in the picture but tear when I bend the board. I would keep a hand check until the supervisor proves the camera catches that fault.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take AI training if offered?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would first ask someone to show me the actual work on paid time. I have never used AI and would need more than a quick video before I trusted a new screen.

say: I would insist on **hand-checking folds** before a camera releases boxes.
I would ask for **paid setup minutes** to remain on the rota.
think: My **junior shift** could shrink as scheduling and stacking change.
Luc’s **road wage** cannot carry the mortgage by itself.
do: Record **four paid setups** and compare the new rota.
Cancel the **summer trip** if paid hours fall.
Look for **posted local packing work** only at bill-covering pay after cuts.
feel: **Anxious** about hours, the mortgage and few nearby alternatives.
S1.quote: I can make the spending cut, but there are few other factories close enough for the school run.
fieldNote: She names a real **household pay gap** if her junior hours fall.
Her first job response is to **look at posted roles**, not claim she has applied or accepted one.

steps.text: Keep current shift and record paid setup time for four runs
Cancel summer trip if paid hours fall
Look for posted local packing jobs at bill-covering pay after cuts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew thinking AI might plan the cartons by 2028 when I am forty five, but capable robots come to the feeder around 2031 when I am forty eight. A screen cannot make those three years feel like a long time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the feeder and stacking jobs to be cut when the robots work reliably. I would lose most of my low wage, and Luc’s road repairs might thin too; our few weeks of savings would not cover the mortgage for long, and I lie awake over it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would stop the trip and other extras now, and ask the plant for its written staffing plan. If my hours were removed, I would apply to any posted nearby factory or packing role with paid safe training and enough wage for our bills; if none appeared, I would ask family about temporary help with the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. The money could run out before I learn a different machine, and thinking about the children’s rooms keeps me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut before asking family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The trip, takeaway meals and the children’s paid club for a term if we had to. I would keep food and the mortgage first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make another job real to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A posted vacancy I can reach after the school drop-off, with pay shown and paid instruction on the machine. A suggestion to retrain without a place is not a job.

say: I would tell the crew **2028 planning AI** precedes hands-on feeder robots around 2031.
I would ask for a **written staffing plan** before the cutter crew is reduced.
think: I expect to lose **most feeder hours** when robots work reliably.
Our **thin reserve** and Luc’s uncertain road work cannot bridge a long mortgage gap.
do: Cut the **trip and extras** before a wage loss arrives.
Apply after **lost hours** only for a posted reachable role with paid safe training and bill-covering wages.
Ask **family for help** if no adequate local opening appears.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected major wage loss and sleepless mortgage worry.
S2.quote: A suggestion to retrain without a place is not a job.
fieldNote: Her alarm rests on **expected major hour loss** plus explicit sleeplessness about the mortgage.
The application requires a **real posting** with reachability, adequate pay and safe paid instruction; family help is a fallback.

steps.text: Cut trip and optional spending before feeder hours fall
Apply after lost hours to posted reachable bill-covering job with paid safe training
Ask family for temporary mortgage help if no adequate opening appears

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say thinking AI arrives in 2031 when I am forty eight, and capable factory robots come around 2034 when I am fifty one. I would ask the plant to tell us about feeder staffing before a machine order is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me time to get the mortgage smaller, but not permission to lose my wage. I would still be raising two children, and our savings would need to grow before a job gap could be safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the current cutter shift, stop the summer trip and put a fresh amount from full weeks into savings after bills. If a nearby packing-machine course is fully funded with paid practice and a posted local job at enough pay, I would enrol and apply after qualifying; otherwise I would keep looking at real vacancies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, though less trapped than in the fast picture. I can learn one machine slowly if someone pays for the time and shows me on the floor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need in a course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: An offered place beside a stopped machine, with a qualified operator showing the guard and emergency stop. The plant must pay the course and the practice hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why not pay for training yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The mortgage is due every month and there is less than a month saved. I would not trade food money for a course without a posted job at a useful wage.

say: I would ask for **feeder staffing figures** before any new machine order.
I would explain **2031 planning AI** arrives before capable physical robots around 2034.
think: The **mortgage** still needs my wage through the warning.
Our **small reserve** must grow before a job gap is manageable.
do: Keep the **die-cutter shift** and cut the summer trip.
Save **new pay** from full weeks after essential bills.
Enrol in **funded paid-time guarded training** only with offered practice and posted bill-covering local work; apply after qualifying.
feel: **Anxious**, but able to try a paid practical route.
S3.quote: I can learn one machine slowly if someone pays for the time and shows me on the floor.
fieldNote: Her plan combines **current wages**, optional spending cuts and genuinely new saving.
The course needs an **offered place**, paid practice, safety instruction and a posted adequate local job; application follows qualification.

steps.text: Keep die-cutter shifts and cancel summer trip
Save fresh pay from full weeks after essential bills
Enrol in funded paid guarded packing course only with offered place and posted bill-covering local job
Apply after qualification for posted nearby bill-covering packing job

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the canteen that thinking AI comes in 2036 when I am fifty three, with capable feeder robots around 2039 when I am fifty six. A mortgage due next month cannot wait thirteen years for a feeder robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our children will be older, but I cannot assume the mortgage or living costs will be gone. I may still need the feeder wage at fifty six, and my thin savings today make it hard to treat a long forecast as safety.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep the paid cutter shifts and write our monthly bills with Luc. In the first year after 2036, if still employed, I would compare paid hours with actual local postings; after a sustained cut I would apply only for a reachable bill-covering job with safe paid instruction, and if there were none I would ask about temporary household support.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about today’s bills and the years after them. I can think about the long date, but the mortgage letter comes now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill do you write down first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The mortgage, then school meals and bus fare. I would not count a future child’s possible wage as money we have today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you promise to work until 2039?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I need wages now, but I cannot predict my health or the plant’s orders at fifty six. I would judge real paid work when that year comes.

say: I would remind the crew **2036 thinking AI** precedes 2039 feeder robots.
I would ask management for **real paid hours**, not a distant promise.
think: The **mortgage** and living costs may still need my wage at fifty six.
Our **thin savings now** keep the household exposed despite the long warning.
do: Keep **paid cutter shifts** now and list monthly bills with Luc.
Apply after **sustained post-2036 cuts** only for reachable bill-covering work with paid safe instruction.
feel: **Anxious** about the mortgage today and later income uncertainty.
S4.quote: A mortgage due next month cannot wait thirteen years for a feeder robot.
fieldNote: Zoe distinguishes **2026 wage need** from conditional employment after 2036.
Her future application requires **lost hours**, a reachable posting, adequate pay and safe paid instruction.

steps.text: Keep paid cutter shifts and list mortgage and school bills now
Apply after sustained cuts for posted reachable bill-covering role with paid safe instruction

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because feeder robots could remove most of my low-paid hours around 2031 while the mortgage still runs. Clear staffing plans, paid practical instruction and posted reachable jobs at bill-covering wages would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what a family does between the last factory shift and the first payment from a different job. The mortgage does not wait for me to become quick with a new screen.

headlineQuote: The mortgage does not wait for me to become quick with a new screen.
portrait: **Zoe**, 43, is a junior cardboard die-cutter operator with secondary schooling and limited confidence with new screens.
Her **low wage**, mortgage, two children, less than a month saved and few nearby factories leave little room for lost shifts.
She has **never used AI** and prefers familiar work, but would consider paid practical training tied to a real job.
Her **baseline anxiety** remains in the plateau, and expected major feeder-hour loss makes the fast case alarming.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove most feeder hours by 2031 while Zoe’s mortgage and school costs continue.
whatWouldHelp: A clear **staffing plan**, paid practical instruction and posted reachable bill-covering jobs would help.
